hn.originalTitle: What Picasso taught me about building AI Agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
What Picasso Taught Me About Building AI Agents — Claramap

The great master Pablo Picasso is famously attributed with saying:

"It took me four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child."

His work, Le Taureau ( The Bull ), captures this beautifully. Across 11 iterations, Picasso progressively stripped away the details of a bull until only a few lines remained. Yet the bull was unmistakable.

In my journey of learning to build AI agents, I can relate. It has come full circle.

Like many engineers, I started with abstractions and sophisticated software systems. Frameworks, orchestration engines, multi-agent architectures, state machines, vector databases, memory systems, and elaborate planning mechanisms.

The more I experimented, the more I found myself stripping things away.

The models were getting better. More things worked with a single prompt. But that wasn't the whole story. I had been overcomplicating things.

This is now my workflow.

I open my terminal.

mkdir my_awesome_agent cd my_awesome_agent claude and start a conversation.

"Claude, I want to build an agent that does XYZ. Help me initialize it. Create an AGENTS.md and let's figure out what else it needs."

I work through a few questions with Claude.

What is this agent supposed to accomplish?

What is the actual job? Not what framework to use, unless you're creating a framework. What does success look like? What decisions can the agent make independently? What should it never do without permission?

What skills does it need?

Skills are specialized instructions that can be reused and remixed. There are plenty of excellent examples on the internet. Borrow them, adapt them, combine them, or ask Claude to create new ones.

Often, a skill is simply a Markdown file with instructions and perhaps a few supporting resources.

What context does it need?

The agent will need context: what your business does, who your customers are, how your codebase works, or some domain-specific knowledge. These can all live as Markdown files inside the folder. Some context can be retrieved when needed. Some comes from the conversation itself. You don't automatically need a vector database or a sophisticated memory architecture.

What tools does it need?

To perform a job, an agent needs tools. Maybe it needs to search the web, read a database, call an API, execute a script, or interact with a browser.

Introducing a tool is as simple as enabling a plugin or adding an MCP connector .

I ask Claude to help identify the smallest set of tools required to accomplish the task. A tool could even be created dynamically, with the agent writing and invoking code. The agent could also find tools on the internet and install them.

How does the agent get invoked?

For an agent to be useful, it needs to be invoked as part of a workflow, whether by a cron job, a webhook event, or another program.

The simplicity is in the packaging. A folder with instructions is a clean deployable unit. It can be versioned, copied around, and embedded in other processes.

With Claude and the required tools and credentials available, it can be invoked headless using the -p flag:

cd my_awesome_agent claude -p "Do awesome stuff" Headless means there is no interactive chat. Claude receives the task, works in the agent's folder, prints the result, and exits. A script can pass in the task and collect the output. For unattended work, I configure the tool permissions in advance. Claude can also return structured JSON for another program to use.

Anthropic's documentation on headless execution covers the commands and configuration.

When the agent starts, it needs to know where to find its instructions, what input it has received, and whether it should resume previous work. The invocation mechanism can change without changing the fundamental purpose of the agent.

This setup can be deployed on a remote VM, with hooks triggering the agent and a tunnel providing access to a service that invokes it.

How does it know whether it has done a good job?

This is where things have drastically improved. I can now get things done with a single prompt, without elaborate instructions. Nowadays, I often just trust it to get on with the job. And I expect it to keep getting better.

When it gets something wrong, I go through it with Claude. What happened? What was missing? What should we change?

hn.titleZh: 畢卡索教我如何建立人工智慧代理
hn.summaryZh: 這篇來自 Hacker News 工程師討論，重點和 Agent 有關。適合用來快速了解社群正在討論的實作方向、工具變化或使用心得。
hn.sourceTextZh:
畢卡索教我如何建立人工智慧代理 — Claramap 偉大的大師巴勃羅·畢加索有一句名言：「我花了四年的時間才畫得像拉斐爾一樣，但花了一生的時間才能畫得像孩子一樣。」他的作品《公牛》完美地捕捉到了這一點。在 11 次迭代中，畢卡索逐漸去除了公牛的細節，直到只剩下幾行線條。然而公牛是毫無疑問的。在我學習建構人工智慧代理的過程中，我能體會這一點。一切又回到了原點。像許多工程師一樣，我從抽象和複雜的軟體系統開始。框架、編排引擎、多代理架構、狀態機、向量資料庫、記憶體系統和複雜的規劃機制。我嘗試的越多，我發現自己剝離的東西就越多。模型變得越來越好。只需一個提示即可完成更多操作。但這還不是故事的全部。我把事情過於複雜化了。這就是我現在的工作流程。我打開我的終端。 mkdir my_awesome_agent cd my_awesome_agent claude 並開始對話。 「Claude，我想建立一個執行 XYZ 功能的代理程式。幫我初始化它。創建一個 AGENTS.md，讓我們弄清楚它還需要什麼。」我和克勞德一起解決了幾個問題。這個代理應該完成什麼任務？實際工作是什麼？不是使用什麼框架，除非你正在創建一個框架。

成功是什麼樣的？代理人可以獨立做出哪些決定？未經許可，它絕對不能做什麼？它需要什麼技能？技能是可以重複使用和重新混合的專門指令。網路上有很多優秀的例子。借用它們、改編它們、組合它們，或要求克勞德創造新的。通常，技能只是一個帶有說明和可能一些支援資源的 Markdown 文件。它需要什麼背景？代理商將需要上下文：您的業務是什麼、您的客戶是誰、您的程式碼庫如何運作或一些特定領域的知識。這些都可以作為 Markdown 檔案存在於資料夾中。需要時可以檢索一些上下文。有些來自對話本身。您並不自動需要向量資料庫或複雜的記憶體架構。它需要什麼工具？為了執行工作，代理需要工具。也許它需要搜尋網路、讀取資料庫、呼叫 API、執行腳本或與瀏覽器互動。引入工具就像啟用插件或添加 MCP 連接器一樣簡單。我請克勞德幫忙確定完成任務所需的最小工具集。甚至可以透過代理程式編寫和呼叫程式碼來動態創建工具。代理還可以在互聯網上找到工具並安裝它們。

代理如何被呼叫？為了使代理程式發揮作用，需要將其作為工作流程的一部分進行調用，無論是透過 cron 作業、Webhook 事件或其他程式。簡單性在於包裝。帶有說明的資料夾是一個乾淨的可部署單元。它可以被版本控制、複製並嵌入其他流程。有了 Claude 以及所需的工具和憑證，就可以使用 -p 標誌來無頭調用它： cd my_awesome_agent claude -p "Do Awesome stuff" 無頭意味著沒有互動式聊天。克勞德收到任務，在代理的資料夾中工作，列印結果，然後退出。腳本可以傳入任務並收集輸出。對於無人值守的工作，我事先配置了工具權限。 Claude 也可以傳回結構化 JSON 以供另一個程式使用。 Anthropic 關於無頭執行的文件涵蓋了命令和設定。當代理程式啟動時，它需要知道在哪裡可以找到它的指令，它收到了什麼輸入，以及是否應該恢復先前的工作。呼叫機制可以改變，而不會改變代理的基本目的。此設定可以部署在遠端虛擬機器上，使用觸發代理的鉤子和提供對呼叫它的服務的存取的隧道。它如何知道自己是否做得很好？這就是事情得到極大改善的地方。

我現在只需一個提示即可完成工作，無需詳細說明。如今，我常常相信它可以完成工作。我預計它會變得越來越好。當出現問題時，我會和克勞德一起解決。發生了什麼事？缺什麼？我們該改變什麼？ Claude 將本機會話記錄保存在 ~/.claude/projects/ / .jsonl 下。每個記錄都會記錄對話、工具呼叫和工具結果。它提供了 h 的踪跡

hn.originalTitle: Amazon MadPot: Honeypot for AI Agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Amazon Threat Intelligence observes threat actors running cybercrime campaigns with ARTEX AI agents | AWS Security Blog

Amazon Threat Intelligence observes threat actors running cybercrime campaigns with ARTEX AI agents

From Oct. 3 to Nov. 5, 2026, Amazon’s MadPot, a globally distributed network of decoy threat sensors, captured requests from AI agents that included operating memory from offensive campaigns that threat actors ran on ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework. The ARTEX agents sent these requests to MadPot sensors configured to present as popular large language model (LLM) inference APIs, and the requests carried the agents’ own records of their campaigns.

Amazon Threat Intelligence assessed threat activity referencing potentially affected AWS customers and notified them as appropriate. Because activity against other organizations could not be confirmed, this post shares the findings and indicators of compromise (IOCs) so that organizations that run the affected technologies can review their own environments.

The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting. Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection. In aggregate, the agent records show that agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention. This post describes how these campaigns operated based on the agents’ own descriptions of the campaigns.

Attribution and instructions

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that ARTEX was used for these campaigns due to prompt references to ARTEX tooling and other technical artifacts referencing ARTEX. Threat actors instructed ARTEX agents through standing instruction prompts that set the mission objectives, targeting rules, and operational constraints. Within those instructions, the agents handled the work themselves. In one credential theft campaign, operators told the agents to work through a fixed sequence of countries, prioritize enterprise production sites over personal projects, and grade every stolen credential by whether it worked and what it could reach. Agents were directed to treat creden.

Amazon Threat Intelligence also assess with moderate confidence these are disparate Chinese-nexus threat groups due to use of simplified Chinese language in prompts, China time-zone configurations, targeting consistent with Chinese interests, and tooling predominantly used by Chinese-nexus threats. Sample instructions included setting red lines, such as excluding mainland China targets and government domains, and required all outbound traffic to go through proxies.

How MadPot saw inside these campaigns

MadPot presents controlled services to potential attackers and records how they discover, test, and attempt to compromise or abuse them. MadPot telemetry allows Amazon Threat Intelligence to observe attacker behavior without exposing customer workloads. In this case, the MadPot sensors presented popular LLM-compatible chat-completions interfaces on various ports. Agentic frameworks sent prompts to these interfaces as part of their offensive workflows, treating them as LLM inference backends.

The resulting telemetry contained the persistent task context, system prompts, tool histories, knowledge-graph state, and reported findings that these frameworks ordinarily send to an LLM to make operational decisions. Because agentic frameworks retain the history of past conversations, individual requests often contain the full operational history of a campaign. That history described activity that occurred before and between the captured requests, on systems MadPot does not monitor. Amazon Threat Intelligence did not observe that activity as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported, but the records show what the actors were pursuing.

Most of the activity used ARTEX to divide work among planner, worker, verification, and compression agents sharing a persistent knowledge graph. The knowledge graph acts as the operation’s shared memory: every agent reads from it, and writes its results back, so each agent picks up where the others left off. hn.titleZh: Amazon MadPot：適用於 AI 代理的蜜罐
hn.summaryZh: 這篇來自 Hacker News 工程師討論，重點和 Agent 有關。適合用來快速了解社群正在討論的實作方向、工具變化或使用心得。
hn.sourceTextZh:
Amazon Threat Intelligence 觀察威脅行為者使用 ARTEX AI 代理程式進行網路犯罪活動 | AWS 安全部落格 Amazon Threat Intelligence 觀察威脅行為者使用 ARTEX AI 代理程式進行網路犯罪活動 2026 年 10 月 3 日至 11 月 5 日，亞馬遜的 MadPot（一個全球分散式裝置在分散式裝置中擷取了一個導向代理程式的工具，亞馬遜的 MadPot（一個全球分散式裝置滲透測試框架）上運行的攻擊活動的操作記憶體。 ARTEX 代理將這些請求傳送到配置為流行的大語言模型 (LLM) 推理 API 的 MadPot 感測器，並且這些請求攜帶代理自己的活動記錄。 Amazon Threat Intelligence 評估了可能受影響的 AWS 客戶的威脅活動，並視情況通知他們。由於無法確認針對其他組織的活動，因此本文分享了調查結果和妥協指標 (IOC)，以便運行受影響技術的組織可以檢查自己的環境。最著名的 ARTEX 活動是大規模盜竊訪問人工智慧模型的憑證，該活動被組織為一項自我維持的行動，其中被盜的密鑰用於支付 LLM 推理費用，從而為進一步的憑證搜尋提供動力。

另一項活動針對加密貨幣交易所，使用即時深度偽造注入繞過了解你的客戶 (KYC) 驗證。總的來說，特工記錄表明，特工框架已經從實驗性使用發展到以最少的人為幹預運作的持續、多目標進攻行動。這篇文章根據代理商自己對活動的描述描述了這些活動是如何運作的。歸因與說明 由於提示引用了 ARTEX 工具和其他引用 ARTEX 的技術工件，Amazon Threat Intelligence 以中等信心評估 ARTEX 用於這些活動。威脅行為者透過常設指令提示來指示 ARTEX 特工，設定任務目標、目標規則和操作限制。根據這些指示，代理人自行處理工作。在一次憑證盜竊活動中，操作員告訴特工在固定的國家/地區序列中工作，優先考慮企業生產站點而不是個人項目，並根據每個被盜憑證是否有效以及可以達到的範圍對每個被盜憑證進行評級。特工被指示治療克雷登。

Amazon Threat Intelligence 也以中等信心評估這些是不同的中國關係威脅群體，因為在提示中使用簡體中文、中國時區配置、目標符合中國利益以及主要由中國關係威脅使用的工具。範例說明包括設定紅線，例如排除中國大陸目標和政府域，並要求所有出站流量都通過代理。 MadPot 如何了解這些活動的內部情況 MadPot 向潛在攻擊者提供受控服務，並記錄他們如何發現、測試以及嘗試破壞或濫用這些服務。 MadPot 遙測可讓 Amazon Threat Intelligence 觀察攻擊者行為，而無需暴露客戶工作負載。在這種情況下，MadPot 感測器在各種連接埠上提供了流行的 LLM 相容的聊天完成介面。代理框架向這些介面發送提示作為其攻擊性工作流程的一部分，將它們視為 LLM 推理後端。產生的遙測資料包含持久任務情境、系統提示、工具歷史記錄、知識圖狀態以及這些框架通常發送給法學碩士以做出營運決策的報告結果。由於代理框架保留了過去對話的歷史記錄，因此單一請求通常包含活動的完整操作歷史記錄。

此歷史記錄描述了在 MadPot 不監控的系統上捕獲的請求之前和之間發生的活動。亞馬遜威脅情報沒有觀察到該活動的發生，也無法驗證特工報告的結果，但記錄顯示了參與者正在追求的目標。大多數活動都使用 ARTEX 在共享持久知識圖譜的規劃器、工作器、驗證和壓縮代理之間劃分工作。知識圖充當操作的共享記憶體：每個智能體都從中讀取數據，並將其結果寫回，因此每個智能體都會從其他智能體停止的地方繼續。特工的記錄描述了跨越 A 的數百個目標的偵察、漏洞測試、憑證盜竊、雲端權限擴展和加密貨幣詐欺嘗試。

hn.originalTitle: Show HN: Attest – Test what AI agents do, not just what they say
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Attest | Attest Framework

Attest 1.1.0 is a testing framework for AI agents in Python and TypeScript. Check a reply, a sequence of tool calls or a change to external state with pytest or Vitest. Start with deterministic checks; add a model judge only for criteria those checks cannot express.

rec → replay → gate

A support agent refunded a customer twice after a payment timeout. Its output-only tests stayed green. That synthetic incident — INC-1042 — becomes a regression test in three moves:

Capture the incident

attest capture records the trace and model exchanges, applies redaction and drafts contracts from the run. A fixture marked consistent with the recording is not proof that the behavior is correct: review the fixture and choose independent business invariants.

Strict replay runs your agent’s real code against recorded model responses through a local proxy, with zero live model calls for matching requests. It removes live-model variability, not other sources of flaky tests; tool dependencies and test isolation still need control.

Checks report pass , fail or not_evaluated with a reason. Failed tests block by default ( tests_failed: block ); not_evaluated warns unless the policy sets not_evaluated: block . Require the policy check in branch protection. The gate covers the contracts and baselines you supply, not every possible regression.

The tour follows the double-refund ledger, reviewed contracts, a blocked revert PR, mutation scores and the HTML viewer. Its outputs illustrate the synthetic demo; the demo README has the current executable walkthrough.

expect ( trace ). tool_cardinality ( " issue_refund " , per = " order_id " , at_most = 1 ) attestExpect (trace) . toolCardinality ( " issue_refund " , { per: " order_id " , atMost: 1 }); One line of behavior contract states the rule INC-1042 broke — over the trace’s tool calls, not the reply text. Six evaluated layers plus plugins Section titled “Six evaluated layers plus plugins” The replay and gate run on deterministic checks. The layers are the full ladder of checks a contract or test can use, from free and instant to LLM-judged. Plugins add your own assertions. The table is generated from attest-engine capabilities --json . 1 Schema validation Checks the output against a JSON Schema. Fr.

experimental : Shipped without a stability commitment and without demonstrated demand; it can change or be removed in any release.

stable : Covered by the parity and conformance suites; a change in behavior is a breaking change.

From attest-engine capabilities --json at engine 1.1.1.

hn.titleZh: Show HN：證明－測試人工智慧代理做了什麼，而不僅僅是他們說了什麼
hn.summaryZh: 這篇來自 Hacker News 工程師討論，重點和 Agent 有關。適合用來快速了解社群正在討論的實作方向、工具變化或使用心得。
hn.sourceTextZh:
證明| Attest 框架 Attest 1.1.0 是 Python 和 TypeScript 中的 AI 代理程式測試框架。使用 pytest 或 Vitest 檢查回應、一系列工具呼叫或外部狀態的變更。從確定性檢查開始；僅針對那些檢查無法表達的標準添加模型法官。記錄 → 重播 → 門 支援代理在付款逾時後兩次為客戶退款。其僅輸出測試保持綠色。此合成事件 - INC-1042 - 通過三個步驟成為回歸測試：捕獲事件證明捕獲記錄追蹤和模型交換，應用修訂並從運行中起草合約。標記與記錄一致的裝置並不能證明行為是正確的：檢查裝置並選擇獨立的業務不變量。嚴格重播透過本地代理根據記錄的模型回應運行代理程式的真實程式碼，匹配請求的即時模型呼叫為零。它消除了即時模型的可變性，而不是其他不穩定測試的來源；工具依賴性和測試隔離仍然需要控制。檢查報告 pass 、 failed 或 not_evaluated 並給出原因。預設失敗的測試會被阻止（tests_failed: block）； not_evaluated 發出警告，除非策略設定 not_evaluated: block 。要求分支保護中的策略檢查。該門涵蓋了您提供的合約和基線，而不是所有可能的回歸。

hn.originalTitle: Amazon Threat Intelligence observes threat actor campaigns with ARTEX AI agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Amazon Threat Intelligence observes threat actors running cybercrime campaigns with ARTEX AI agents | AWS Security Blog

Amazon Threat Intelligence observes threat actors running cybercrime campaigns with ARTEX AI agents

From Oct. 3 to Nov. 5, 2026, Amazon’s MadPot, a globally distributed network of decoy threat sensors, captured requests from AI agents that included operating memory from offensive campaigns that threat actors ran on ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework. The ARTEX agents sent these requests to MadPot sensors configured to present as popular large language model (LLM) inference APIs, and the requests carried the agents’ own records of their campaigns.

Amazon Threat Intelligence assessed threat activity referencing potentially affected AWS customers and notified them as appropriate. Because activity against other organizations could not be confirmed, this post shares the findings and indicators of compromise (IOCs) so that organizations that run the affected technologies can review their own environments.

The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting. Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection. In aggregate, the agent records show that agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention. This post describes how these campaigns operated based on the agents’ own descriptions of the campaigns.

Attribution and instructions

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that ARTEX was used for these campaigns due to prompt references to ARTEX tooling and other technical artifacts referencing ARTEX. Threat actors instructed ARTEX agents through standing instruction prompts that set the mission objectives, targeting rules, and operational constraints. Within those instructions, the agents handled the work themselves. In one credential theft campaign, operators told the agents to work through a fixed sequence of countries, prioritize enterprise production sites over personal projects, and grade every stolen credential by whether it worked and what it could reach. Agents were directed to treat creden.

Amazon Threat Intelligence also assess with moderate confidence these are disparate Chinese-nexus threat groups due to use of simplified Chinese language in prompts, China time-zone configurations, targeting consistent with Chinese interests, and tooling predominantly used by Chinese-nexus threats. Sample instructions included setting red lines, such as excluding mainland China targets and government domains, and required all outbound traffic to go through proxies.

How MadPot saw inside these campaigns

MadPot presents controlled services to potential attackers and records how they discover, test, and attempt to compromise or abuse them. MadPot telemetry allows Amazon Threat Intelligence to observe attacker behavior without exposing customer workloads. In this case, the MadPot sensors presented popular LLM-compatible chat-completions interfaces on various ports. Agentic frameworks sent prompts to these interfaces as part of their offensive workflows, treating them as LLM inference backends.

The resulting telemetry contained the persistent task context, system prompts, tool histories, knowledge-graph state, and reported findings that these frameworks ordinarily send to an LLM to make operational decisions. Because agentic frameworks retain the history of past conversations, individual requests often contain the full operational history of a campaign. That history described activity that occurred before and between the captured requests, on systems MadPot does not monitor. Amazon Threat Intelligence did not observe that activity as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported, but the records show what the actors were pursuing.

Most of the activity used ARTEX to divide work among planner, worker, verification, and compression agents sharing a persistent knowledge graph. The knowledge graph acts as the operation’s shared memory: every agent reads from it, and writes its results back, so each agent picks up where the others left off. The agents’ records described reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, credential theft, cloud-privilege expansion, and cryptocurrency fraud attempts across hundreds of targets spanning A

hn.sourceTextZh:
Amazon Threat Intelligence 觀察威脅行為者使用 ARTEX AI 代理程式進行網路犯罪活動 | AWS 安全部落格 Amazon Threat Intelligence 觀察威脅行為者使用 ARTEX AI 代理程式進行網路犯罪活動 2026 年 10 月 3 日至 11 月 5 日，亞馬遜的 MadPot（一個全球分散式裝置在分散式裝置中擷取了一個導向代理程式的工具，亞馬遜的 MadPot（一個全球分散式裝置滲透測試框架）上運行的攻擊活動的操作記憶體。 ARTEX 代理將這些請求傳送到配置為流行的大語言模型 (LLM) 推理 API 的 MadPot 感測器，並且這些請求攜帶代理自己的活動記錄。 Amazon Threat Intelligence 評估了可能受影響的 AWS 客戶的威脅活動，並視情況通知他們。由於無法確認針對其他組織的活動，因此本文分享了調查結果和妥協指標 (IOC)，以便運行受影響技術的組織可以檢查自己的環境。最著名的 ARTEX 活動是大規模盜竊訪問人工智慧模型的憑證，該活動被組織為一項自我維持的行動，其中被盜的密鑰用於支付 LLM 推理費用，從而為進一步的憑證搜尋提供動力。

另一項活動針對加密貨幣交易所，使用即時深度偽造注入繞過了解你的客戶 (KYC) 驗證。總的來說，特工記錄表明，特工框架已經從實驗性使用發展到以最少的人為幹預運作的持續、多目標進攻行動。這篇文章根據代理商自己對活動的描述描述了這些活動是如何運作的。歸因與說明 由於提示引用了 ARTEX 工具和其他引用 ARTEX 的技術工件，Amazon Threat Intelligence 以中等信心評估 ARTEX 用於這些活動。威脅行為者透過常設指令提示來指示 ARTEX 特工，設定任務目標、目標規則和操作限制。根據這些指示，代理人自行處理工作。在一次憑證盜竊活動中，操作員告訴特工在固定的國家/地區序列中工作，優先考慮企業生產站點而不是個人項目，並根據每個被盜憑證是否有效以及可以達到的範圍對每個被盜憑證進行評級。特工被指示治療克雷登。

Amazon Threat Intelligence 也以中等信心評估這些是不同的中國關係威脅群體，因為在提示中使用簡體中文、中國時區配置、目標符合中國利益以及主要由中國關係威脅使用的工具。範例說明包括設定紅線，例如排除中國大陸目標和政府域，並要求所有出站流量都通過代理。 MadPot 如何了解這些活動的內部情況 MadPot 向潛在攻擊者提供受控服務，並記錄他們如何發現、測試以及嘗試破壞或濫用這些服務。 MadPot 遙測可讓 Amazon Threat Intelligence 觀察攻擊者行為，而無需暴露客戶工作負載。在這種情況下，MadPot 感測器在各種連接埠上提供了流行的 LLM 相容的聊天完成介面。代理框架向這些介面發送提示作為其攻擊性工作流程的一部分，將它們視為 LLM 推理後端。產生的遙測資料包含持久任務情境、系統提示、工具歷史記錄、知識圖狀態以及這些框架通常發送給法學碩士以做出營運決策的報告結果。由於代理框架保留了過去對話的歷史記錄，因此單一請求通常包含活動的完整操作歷史記錄。

此歷史記錄描述了在 MadPot 不監控的系統上捕獲的請求之前和之間發生的活動。亞馬遜威脅情報沒有觀察到該活動的發生，也無法驗證特工報告的結果，但記錄顯示了參與者正在追求的目標。大多數活動都使用 ARTEX 在共享持久知識圖譜的規劃器、工作器、驗證和壓縮代理之間劃分工作。知識圖充當操作的共享記憶體：每個智能體都從中讀取數據，並將其結果寫回，因此每個智能體都會從其他智能體停止的地方繼續。特工的記錄描述了跨越 A 的數百個目標的偵察、漏洞測試、憑證盜竊、雲端權限擴展和加密貨幣詐欺嘗試。

hn.originalTitle: ChatGPT Desktop forwards your SSH agent to remote machines
hn.sourceOriginalText:
The agent running on a remote machine can authenticate using your local SSH credentials. That means it can push to your private repos on GitHub, for example. Proof: https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28131#discussion_r3410013180

Comment 1: I'd suggest to use ssh keys inside the secure enclave on macOS that require your fingerprint for every new session [0]. That way agents cannot initiate anything, and you will always be aware when a new ssh connection is being made. [0]: https://gist.github.com/arianvp/5f59f1783e3eaf1a2d4cd8e952bb...

Comment 2: Or in a Yubikey and set the touch-required mechanism (light in the key will blink when it needs a touch to continue the auth).

Comment 3: I've been using secretive on the mac for exactly this.

Comment 4: Secretive is amazing! I know that it's not its purpose, but it would be great if it could store more than ssh keys, like providing a safe place for my .envs

hn.originalTitle: Show HN: Thrum – run Claude Code, Codex and other coding agents as one team
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Thrum

Stop babysitting your coding agents. They check each other's work, so you can trust what reaches you.

Your agents message each other, even when they run on different tools: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more. No more pasting one agent's answer into another's window. Start with two: a coordinator you talk to, and a reviewer it creates when you ask. When the work grows, add agents and keep talking to one. You get decisions, not diffs to chase.

Free costs nothing and needs no account.

Start your free 14-day trial today. No card for the trial. When it ends, Thrum goes back to Free and your data stays.

Free costs nothing and needs no account: your agents message each other, you talk to them in their own terminals or message them from My Inbox, and you watch them in the web UI. Pro is $15.00/month or $120.00/year. It lets you type to your agents from the web UI and lets them write memory and a work queue.

Your browser cannot play this video. Download the walkthrough (MP4) .

You type one request to your coordinator. It hands the work to Codex. A reviewer on a different model checks Codex's work, and the coordinator approves the reviewer's permission prompt for you. Then you get a report to decide on. The walkthrough is narrated and just over two minutes; it opens with a short look at the console.

Here the coordinator is set to ask you before it merges. By default it merges routine changes itself. Agent work is sped up in places. Recorded with Thrum Pro, which adds the work queue the coordinator uses to keep track of your request. Captions are available.

Agents check each other's work

An agent saying "done" is a claim, not a result. In Thrum, the claim is checked before it reaches you.

Your coordinator reviews each branch, and before it pushes a merge it's set up to build and test the merged result. You choose whether it asks you before each merge or merges routine changes itself.

Add a gate agent, an agent whose job is to run your tests on that merged code. Its verdict says what it measured and what it didn't. If no gate agent checked a merge, the record says so.

The agents that write the code (implementers) are told to start from a failing test, so a fix has something to prove.

In the video above, a reviewer on a different model reports two minor findings, and the coordinator confirms neither needs a change before anything reaches you.

If you run more than one coding agent

You don't need several agents already. Two are enough to start, and each one can run on whichever AI tool and model you choose.

You're the one carrying messages between them, checking what each one says it did, and remembering who is waiting on whom. With Thrum, they message each other, a reviewer checks what they say they did, and you talk to one coordinator.

Thrum is for developers running more than one coding agent on real code, who want to stay the one who decides. With two or three agents, Free has everything your agents need to work as a team. It costs nothing and needs no account. If your project is in a public repository, Pro is free too, for each one you register, as long as it stays public. You need a free account for that. How to get it

Many AI tools let one agent hand work to its own subagents or team. Thrum's messages go between full agents, each in its own session, on whichever supported tool it runs, and to you. If one agent and its helpers cover your work, you may not need more. Thrum is excellent when your agents run on more than one tool, or when you want one coordinator to talk to and an inbox of your own.

If you'd rather not build it yourself

If you want this functionality, you can build it yourself today. Claude Code is good at that, but you have to build it yourself, and you have to troubleshoot it. Thrum gives it to you out of the box, and that part is free.

Your agents deploy, too

Ask your coordinator to add a deployer. It runs your scripted deploys. It's set up to deploy dev and staging on its own and to ask your coordinator before production. Afterwards it checks the deploy and reports back. Your AI tool runs your own deploy commands and cloud tools.

When your AI tool asks permission to run a command, Thrum tells you. Answer from the web inbox or Telegram, which are free, or by replying to an email with Pro. Thrum types your answer into the agent's terminal.

What Thrum takes off your plate

Answer your agents’ questions once, from one place

Write to your coordinator in plain words and it passes your req

hn.originalTitle: Ask HN: How do you evaluate the skills your AI agents use?
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Do you systematically evaluate agent skills, either before or while using them? If so, what tools or methods do you use? Or do you mostly rely on reading the SKILL.md and trying things out?

Comment 1: There are two ways I see to do this: 1. Tell your agent to eval the skill itself ( https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals ). This is easier and faster, but less accurate, and harder to extend to capture things like code quality. 2. Build your own benchmark out of work your normally do, and then eval the skill on that dataset. This is harder and more annoying (because creating benchmarks is hard) but provides deeper insight into how the skill affects the agent in known scenarios. It also depends on what the skill is doing. If it's creating an artifact (like a report, easier to eval) then your strategy is very different than if the skill is changing agent behavior (like telling it to use cheap subagents under XYZ conditions, harder to eval). The importance of doing this grows with the number of people using the skill. Working on my own projects, I don't usua.

Comment 2: Would you know of decent sources on creating (personal mostly) benchmarks? Doing something like that currently for processing PDFs and it's a bit cumbersome, but that's work I guess.

Comment 3: This article should is a good source for getting started in the space https://every.to/also-true-for-humans/how-to-create-your-own... My 2c as someone who is working on this problem is that you can follow the 80/20 rule when making them for personal use - put in the 20% and you can make a good enough benchmark relatively easily. The remaining work is certainly valuable, and necessary to do if the benchmark is consequential, but it's a pain in the ass and hard to do correctly, so if you don't have to, don't worry about it

Comment 4: Thank you, will give it a read.
hn.titleZh: Q HN：您如何評估 AI 代理程式使用的技能？
hn.summaryZh: 這篇來自 Hacker News 工程師討論，重點和 Agent 有關。適合用來快速了解社群正在討論的實作方向、工具變化或使用心得。
hn.sourceTextZh:
您是否在使用代理技能之前或使用過程中系統地評估它們？如果是這樣，您使用什麼工具或方法？或者您主要依賴閱讀 SKILL.md 並進行嘗試？評論 1：我認為有兩種方法可以做到這一點： 1. 告訴您​​的代理評估技能本身（https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals）。這更容易、更快，但不太準確，並且更難擴展以捕獲程式碼品質等內容。 2. 根據您通常所做的工作建立您自己的基準，然後評估該資料集的技能。這更難、更煩人（因為創建基準很困難），但可以更深入地了解該技能在已知場景中如何影響代理。這也取決於技能的用途。如果它正在創建一個工件（例如報告，更容易評估），那麼您的策略與技能改變代理行為（例如告訴它在 XYZ 條件下使用便宜的子代理，更難評估）有很大不同。這樣做的重要性隨著使用該技能的人數的增加而增加。我不習慣做自己的專案。評論 2：您知道創建（主要是個人）基準的可靠來源嗎？目前處理 PDF 時做類似的事情有點麻煩，但我想這就是工作。

評論 3：這篇文章應該是一個很好的入門資源 https://every.to/also-true-for- humans/how-to-create-your-own... 作為正在解決這個問題的人，我的 2c 是，你可以在製作供個人使用時遵循 80/20 規則 - 放入 20%，你可以相對輕鬆地制定一個足夠好的基準。剩下的工作當然是有價值的，如果基準測試是重要的，那麼就有必要做，但是這是一件痛苦的事情，而且很難正確地完成，所以如果你不需要，不要擔心它評論 4：謝謝你，會讀一下。
